title: Generic Interface Functions
story: You built a `Displayable` interface and implemented it for Books, Movies, and Songs. Now you want to write ONE function that prints a list of ANY displayable items - not three separate functions. Generics + interfaces is the answer.
why: Generic functions with interface bounds let you write code that works on any type implementing a given interface, eliminating duplicate functions.
analogy: A vending machine accepts any coin - pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters - because they all satisfy the 'Currency' interface. The machine doesn't need separate slots for each coin type. Generic functions work the same way: one slot for any type that satisfies the interface.
try_it: Add a `summarize_all[T: Displayable](items: &Vec[T]) -> Str` function that combines all display strings with commas. Then add a `Snack` type that implements Displayable and pass it to both functions.
tips: `fn f[T: Interface](x: T)` reads as: 'for any T that implements Interface'
The compiler generates a separate optimized version for each concrete type used
You can require multiple interfaces: `T: A + B + C`
common_mistakes: Writing separate functions for each type instead of one generic function
Forgetting that `items.get(i)` returns `Option`, needing `.unwrap()` or match
Trying to call interface methods on a type that doesn't implement the interface
